Thirteen die in the three towns that night, including Hieronymous ("It would tear your heart out of your breast to see it!") and Hilary.

Hieronymous had predicted: "I will not survive. I will be the scapegoat. That is my role." But why these two specifically? Both are Americans, both intellectuals, both among those who most fully grasped the unreality of the world. Perhaps their very understanding made them vulnerable—or perhaps the locusts simply select at random from among "the rarified ones filled with air."

Solomon's Legitimacy

Is Solomon truly a Giant, or a fraud who gamed the system?

Solomon bribes the Ifrit (with "a bribe so small") to announce him as the "Riant Giant." Gorgonius reveals that even if Solomon were Atrox's legitimate successor, he would become the Bottom Giant, not the Top. Atrox's ghost finally assigns Solomon the Patagonian position—"the lowest and least" of the seven.

Yet Solomon does become a Giant. He was "untimely born the second time, out of the belly-button of his brother." Saint Faunus explains that untimely second birth qualifies one for giantship. Solomon's father is Iofel the Trickster Angel. He alone can enter the Fountain of Youth.

The question: Did Solomon earn his position through cunning, inherit it through supernatural parentage, or was he always fated to be exactly what he becomes—the smallest giant, the bottom of the hierarchy, yet still genuinely a Pillar of the World?

The Unreality Thesis

Is the world actually unreal, or is this a metaphor?

"To be real is to be unique. To be unreal is to be common. And the odds in favor of the world being unreal are prohibitive. There is only one chance in all infinity of it being real." Hilary's fish business works without fish. Denis's forgeries perform miracles. Jane can write birds and trees into existence.

Yet the "lumpenproletariat"—80% of the video conference audience—pass Atrox's tests as wide-awake. Alexander the Great says "reality must be earned" and that unreality is "more the rule than the exception" beyond the civilized core.

The puzzle: Lafferty seems to be saying something about creativity, authorship, and the constructed nature of reality—but what? Is the unreality literal (we live in a Giant's dream) or figurative (civilization is a shared fiction maintained by extraordinary people)? The novel refuses to settle the question.

The Kabouters and the Little People

What is the relationship between the Kabouters, the Sioga, and humanity?

Laughter-Lynn is partly "of the Kabouter blood" through her father Fernand Kabouter Casement. The documents she reads describe the "Puka, the Sioga, the Goblins, the Kabouter, the Little People, the Fairies, the Lamiae" as having their own Eden (named Gaire/Laughter) eleven years before the human Eden. The old lady Gioia and old man Timore belong to "the hobgoblin people, the gnomes, the eldritch-elves, the puka people."

These beings seem to coexist with humanity as a parallel population, sometimes interbreeding (Laughter-Lynn), sometimes serving as witnesses to giant activity. Their precise cosmological status—are they real where humans are unreal? older? more authentic?—remains unclear.

The Number Seven

Why does seven recur throughout?

Seven Scribbling Giants. Seven Saints. Seven Technicians. Seven days of the week (plus the Eighth and Ninth). The "Seven New Giants" (Sussex Wraiths). Seven steam calliopes. Seven flutes. The seven shadow shootings.

The number has obvious biblical resonance (days of creation, seals of Revelation) and appears in virtually every mythological system. Lafferty deploys it both seriously (the cosmic structure of Pillars) and comically (the New Giants who turn out to be "bats").

Unresolved Plot Threads

Minor mysteries the novel leaves open:
  • Who sent Prince Leonardo in the crate, and why?
  • What happened to the totem pole spirits—will they be freed?
  • Does Denis's Laughing Christ continue to house Saint Faunus, or did Faunus die completely in the rock slide?
  • What is Monika's true role—why does she possess both the forged and true Aladdin's Lamps?
  • Will the buried player pianos at Sora truly play "forever"?
  • What becomes of Perpetua, now widowed and bereaved of her father's full attention?
  • Does the world remain stable with its new Giants, or is another crisis inevitable?

Atrox's Fifteen Hundred Years

How can Atrox be both dead and writing new chapters?

Atrox "die[s] on the evening of the last day" of year 453. Yet new chapters arrive regularly, "delivered by somebody known and accepted by our savage dogs." When asked what year he lives in, the ghost-Atrox replies: "I live yet in the year of restored salvation four hundred and fifty-three, the last year I may live in... The world exterior to me, however, is now about twelve years beyond me."

He says he has "written the world to about the year two thousand, though the world itself has not yet moved into my scenario of it all the way." So he writes the future from the past, his death not preventing his continued authorship.

The puzzle: Is this time-loop a feature of Giant existence? Does being a Scribbling Giant mean one exists outside normal causation? Or is Atrox's continued writing simply what it means to be a world-author—the text survives the author?

The Charlemagne Episode

Did Atrox invent Charlemagne?

Sandra Ott of the casual English Intellectuals argues: "The Charlemagne Episode fits illy into European history. Its texture is just not the same at all. The supposed contemporaries of Charlemagne never heard of him. Tear the whole Charlemagne Episode out of European history and it leaves no hole at all."

This is vintage Lafferty provocation—suggesting that a major historical epoch might be a Giant's fiction inserted into the world's narrative. The idea echoes his treatment of "phantom time" hypotheses and alternative histories in other works. Is this a joke? A genuine alternative-history speculation? An illustration of what "writing the world" might mean?

Chapter-by-Chapter Reading Notes

These notes highlight key moments, recurring motifs, and passages worth close attention on re-reading.

Chapter 1: "Are We Dreaming?"

Key passages: The Alpine Giant's epigraph explaining the Three-Seven structure of the Pillars; Hilary's discovery that the fish business proves unreality; the introduction of Solomon as "grotesque brilliant growth"; the poltergeist-inhabited computers.

Pay attention to: The phrase "To be real is to be unique. To be unreal is to be common"—this is the novel's philosophical core. Also note the family motto "When you have a good thing going, don't ask questions."

Chapter 2: "Camel's Nose"

Key passages: The Erasthenos epigraph on wanton giants; Laughter-Lynn's double birth and the Shoga boarding school; Leo's discovery of the bloody feather; the Auctore fragment about Atrox.

Pay attention to: The phrase "Atrox has intruded his slurpy wet Camel's nose into the tent of this account and soon will own the place." Lafferty signals that Atrox is becoming author of the novel we're reading.

Chapter 3: "Strange Cargo"

Key passages: The Hebrews epigraph about entertaining angels unaware; Prince Leonardo's arrival "from the Exterior Darkness"; the seven shadow shootings; the conversation about whether there is "organization out there."

Pay attention to: Leonardo's Green Pasture Counselling Service—his genuine care for troubled souls makes his later murders more troubling. Also: "Deadly, deadly, deadly!" about Leonardo's shadow.

Chapter 4: "Monday at Sora"

Key passages: Alexander the Great's interview in the catacombs—"Reality is not something that one has the right and title to. It is something that must be earned"; Atrox's outline appearance and warning; the nine-gallon drinking cup.

Pay attention to: Alexander calls Atrox "altogether second class." This matters—even the great Giant is mediocre by world-historical standards.

Chapter 5: "Tuesday at Gaire Castle"

Key passages: Jane Chantal's murder—"The wonderful screaming of Jane Chantal Ardri rose like an arrow"; the earthquake burying Sora; Saint Brandon's lens-shaped earth cosmography; Drusilla carrying Atrox across the moat.

Pay attention to: The Countess Maude's whispered secret to Hilary—she knows something about Atrox's relationship to Jane's original creation. Also: "It wasn't the first or the second indication that the world was unreal, but it was one of the most telling."

Chapter 6: "Wednesday at Oosterend"

Key passages: The undersea journey via the Circular Stairway; Captain Cornelius's account of Saint Joseph; the drowned-man conversations; Atrox's explanation of his writing method; Atrox's murder at midnight.

Pay attention to: "You are a dozen or more from among the six thousand characters I have written to represent the six-billion persons who will have lived in the world after my death." The Group of Twelve are Atrox's creations—or are they?

Chapter 7: "Thursday at East Sussex"

Key passages: The triple epigraph (Tocquet, Shelley, Eliot); Hilary confronting the Strange Man; the Seven New Giants with their dead-goose feathers; Jane's warnings about the "murder house."

Pay attention to: "This house becomes a murder house now... All of you people must stay very close together or you will be picked off and killed one by one." Jane's warnings prove prophetic.

Chapter 8: "Friday at Port Saint Mary"

Key passages: The Dublin Docket articles on world-strangulation; Leonardo's murder of John Barkley; the hanging and revelation of the Strange Man; the Night of Strangulation.

Pay attention to: John Barkley's premonition: "I know that this is my death-day." The scientific-journalistic style of the world-crisis reporting parodies both academic papers and sensational journalism.

Chapter 9: "Saturday at Lecco"

Key passages: Charles Fort's explanation of the Fortean Universe and 109-year locusts; the rock slide killing Leo, Laughter-Lynn, and Saint Faunus; the mourning and decisions about clearance; Solomon's entry into the Fountain of Youth.

Pay attention to: "Leo wasn't meant to grow up. Now he can be a Boy Genius forever." Perpetua's refusal to clear the rocks reflects a very Laffertian acceptance of death.

Chapter 10: "Sunday at Klavierschloss"

Key passages: The Psalm epigraph paired with the Irish folk song about burying Laughing Kelly; the Alpine Giant's request to die; Gorgonius accepting giantship; the Ifrit's "Habemus Gigantem."

Pay attention to: The mourning scenes and the Alpine Giant's card game with Perpetua—"Only you could do that." The transition from grief to cosmic appointment is quintessentially Laffertian.

Chapter 11: "At the Eighth Day of the Week"

Key passages: The Dead's perspective—"Why worry about life? It's only temporary"; the Wall Street Journal (Eighth Day Edition) on metaphor and mythology; Solomon's business empire revealed; the succession crisis.

Pay attention to: The dead treat life as "a minor early experience." This reversal of perspective is the novel's deepest joke and perhaps its deepest wisdom.

Chapter 12: "On the Ninth Day of the Week"

Key passages: The Riant Giant's 100-foot projection; the Top Giant paradox—"The successor to the Top Giant is never the new Top Giant: he's the new Bottom Giant"; Solomon's acceptance of the Patagonian position; the final spherical grin.

Pay attention to: Solomon's business card: "SOLOMON IZZERSTED THE PATAGONIAN GIANT. I DO FUTURES." And the novel's last line: "And his spherical grin spread until it included all of him."
